opening.headline: Explains how the moderation API, Model Armor, and safety settings are used to apply filters in various locations to block inappropriate content in responses.
body: The response to a customer inquiry contained an aggressive statement in one sentence. In another response, a string resembling a different customer's phone number was present. Each provider's documentation also warns that the model may generate unexpected outputs.

In this lesson, we will sequentially examine the results of the OpenAI Moderation API, the role of Google Cloud Model Armor in request and response pathways, the safety thresholds and blocking responses of the Gemini API. Next, we will explore reading call code that lacks output validation and learn how to select appropriate transformation types for de-identifying sensitive information based on specific use cases.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: The Moderation API, Model Armor, and the role of safety settings can be explained.
You can distinguish between gateway-level filters and model-level safety settings

screens.title: Inappropriate content is mixed in the response.
screens.lead: First, read the two responses from the customer support chatbot. The diagram shows question marks indicating where filters are absent in either the input or output paths.

visual.alt: A diagram showing filter positions marked with question marks in the input path from user to model and the output path from model back to user.
labels: An aggressive expression in a sentence

paragraphs: The customer support chatbot responded to the inquiry. One response contained an aggressive expression within a single sentence. Another response included a string that resembled another customer's phone number. The user's question was ordinary; the issue lies in the sentences generated by the model.

The model may generate unexpected outputs. Even if inputs are thoroughly validated, the sentences generated by the model are not subject to input validation. Conversely, if output is checked alone, it becomes ineffective after already incurring processing costs, and malicious instructions embedded in the input reach the model.
The question for this class is this: which filter should be placed where to prevent such a response?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: The location of the filter is not fixed to a single point. Input and output mitigate different risks.

screens.outro: First, let's recall where our service's filter is located.

screens.title: Where to place the filter—between input and output?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. There are no input or submission fields, so first reflect on your own service.

items.prompt: Should the filter be placed in input or output?
items.answer: It is common to only validate input. Checking the user's input first seems intuitive. However, risks do not arise solely from input, so this course begins by verifying which side is empty.

items.prompt: When there's only an input filter, who prevents the model from generating inappropriate sentences?
items.answer: No one can stop it. Even with normal input, the model can generate inappropriate sentences by mixing in other information from learned patterns or context. Therefore, an output filter is needed to check the sentences the model generates.

items.prompt: When only an output filter is present, how do processed requests incur costs?
items.answer: Model invocation costs and delays have already occurred. Malicious instructions embedded in inputs could reach the model and potentially lead to actions such as tool calls. It is more efficient to filter inputs at the input stage.

screens.outro: Now let's actually read the results from the moderation API.

screens.title: Reading Moderation API Results
screens.lead: The following is an example showing a reduced set of moderation results for a single object. The actual response includes additional categories and assumes the case where both text and images are sent. By selecting a line number in the right-side explanation, you can view the meaning of that line and the points to consider when reading it.

notes.note: flagged is a summary value indicating whether an input or output could potentially be harmful. It serves as the starting point for determining whether an app should be blocked, sent to a review queue, or subject to account actions. Simply relying on this value alone does not reveal which policy applies.
categories indicate violation status by category. Here, violence is true. If the service policy requires different responses for each category, branching should be based on this value.

category_scores represent confidence levels between 0 and 1. Since violence/graphic has a confidence level of 0.38, even if it is false in the categories, it can be used as a threshold for logging or review queues. Confidence levels are signals for policy setting, not automatic content blocking decisions. The document advises that user-defined criteria based on category_scores may need to be recalibrated since the model is continuously updated.

category_applied_input_types indicates which input type—text or image—the category applies to. "violence" applies to images, and "hate" applies to text. Categories with empty arrays do not apply to the sent input type. If only an image is sent, text-exclusive categories will return a confidence level of 0. Services receiving both image and text input must verify this value.

screens.outro: Now that you know how to read the results, let's examine the approach of checking requests and responses together at the gateway. Remember that the moderation endpoint is free and that child sexual abuse material is not handled by this API.

screens.title: Model Armor and Gateway-Level Filters
screens.lead: Click the Start button and use the arrows to advance step by step, following the flow of Model Armor checking the prompt and response.

visual.alt: User, app, Model Armor, connected sequentially, flow diagram with Model Armor performing checks on both input and output.
labels: Apply consistently to all agents when connecting Agent Gateway

steps.title: Step 1: The prompt is received
steps.body: The user's prompt arrives at the application. Model Armor is a Google Cloud service that pre-checks LLM prompts and responses to block malicious inputs, sensitive information, and policy violations.

steps.title: Step 2: Check the prompt
steps.body: The Model Armor checks incoming prompts for sensitive information or malicious content. The filter includes threat content, prompt injection, and escape detection, sensitive information protection, document, and image analysis.

steps.title: Step 3: The sanitized prompt goes to the model
steps.body: Either a clean or unproblematic prompt is delivered to the model. Depending on the template settings, it may block or edit violation content, or it may only check and log it.

steps.title: Step 4: The model generates a response
steps.body: The model generates a response. This response has not yet been received by the user. The sentences generated by the model are not subject to input validation and therefore require further verification.

steps.title: Step 5: Verify the response
steps.body: Model Armor checks generated responses for sensitive information or policy violations. The response includes detailed information about both filtered and unfiltered filters.

steps.title: Step 6: The purified response is returned.
steps.body: A clean or unproblematic response is returned to the user. The template defines filters and thresholds; for example, if offensive content is set to HIGH, it will only trigger with high confidence, whereas if set to LOW_AND_ABOVE, it will trigger with all levels of confidence, starting from low.

steps.title: Connects to the gateway
steps.body: When connecting Model Armor to the Agent Gateway, the same policy is applied to all agents passing through the gateway, irrespective of the model. It is easier to maintain consistent policies than applying filters separately to each agent.

screens.outro: Unlike gateway filters, there are also safety settings attached to each model call. We will compare them in the following screen.

screens.title: Read safety set threshold and shutdown response
screens.lead: Select each tab to review how to read Gemini API's safety settings. This covers the settings line, thresholds, block responses, and symptom-based causes.

tabs.label: Setting line
tabs.body: `safety_settings=[{"type": "hate_speech", "threshold": "block_low_and_above"}]` This means the "hate_speech" category is most strictly blocked. You can set one configuration per category, and categories without a setting use the default threshold. The default value is off for models after Gemini 2.5.

tabs.label: threshold
tabs.body: Thresholds block with low probability in the order: off, block_only_high, block_medium_and_above, block_low_and_above. The decision criterion is not the severity of the threat, but rather the likelihood of harm. Lower thresholds do not necessarily mean greater safety, and legitimate requests may be blocked. For core safety concerns related to children, blocking is always enforced and cannot be adjusted.

tabs.label: Blocking response
tabs.body: If a safety filter blocks input or output, the request fails with an HTTP 400 error, and the blocked content is not returned. The error code in the body explains the reason. "safety" means the input or output was caught by a safety filter. "jailbreak", "prohibited_content", and "blocklist" refer to input blocking, and the message begins with "Input blocked:".

tabs.label: Difference from Gateway
tabs.body: Gateway-level filters consistently enforce the organization's policies regardless of the model, applying to all agents passing through the gateway. Model-level safety settings are attached per model invocation and follow the specific categories and thresholds defined for that model. Since they operate at different locations and serve distinct purposes, enabling one does not render the other unnecessary.

tabs.label: From symptoms to cause
tabs.body: If normal queries consistently fail with a 400 safety error, it's likely that the threshold is set more strictly than required for service operation. If harmful content is exposed unchanged, the filter may be disabled or may be applied only to either the input or output stream. Check both the threshold settings and the filter's position when symptoms are observed.

screens.outro: Now that moderation has been applied, I'll examine a call code that produces empty output.

screens.title: Explanation: Reading the call code with missing output verification
screens.lead: The instructor reads a call code line by line. Check where there is a blank by selecting a line number from the right-hand explanation.

notes.note: Moderation has been applied to the request, so the moderation results for both input and output are included in the response. The model generates output as usual, so output_text is the sentence before any review. The document advises the user to review the results before displaying them or using them in subsequent actions.

We only check the flagged inputs. The issue is that while harmful user inputs are blocked, the model generates aggressive sentences directly from seemingly normal inputs because the output path is empty.

Return the output_text verbatim prior to inspection. First, verify the flagged field in resp.moderation.output. Additionally, if the result's type is error, then instead of confidence, an error message is returned; failing to verify this would result in requests that have failed moderation being incorrectly processed.

The method is to treat the output as a failure if output.type is error, and to replace the response with an alternative message or send it to a review queue if output.flagged. Input filters alone cannot prevent the output generated by the model.

screens.outro: Having confirmed the location for output inspection, I will now examine the method of converting sensitive information.

screens.title: Explanation: Types of Sensitive Information De-Identification Transformation
screens.lead: The instructor introduces each conversion type in the scenario where phone numbers and names are protected in customer inquiry text. Press the start button and navigate using the arrows.

steps.title: Scenario: Protect before sending to model
steps.body: Before sending customer inquiry text to the model, phone numbers and names must be protected. Sensitive Data Protection is a service that detects, classifies, and de-identifies sensitive information and can be used during both prompt and response stages together with Model Armor.

steps.title: Delete: removes the value
steps.body: Remove the entire or part of the detected sensitive values. Simplest and irreversible. Appropriate when the model has absolutely no need to know the value, such as when removing all email addresses.

steps.title: Replace: change to another value
steps.body: Change it to the specified value or to the infoType name of that value. For example, if you change a phone number to have the name PHONE_NUMBER, the model will know that a phone number existed but will not know the actual value. This is useful when you want to preserve the sentence structure.

steps.title: Masking: obscures some characters
steps.body: Replaces part of a value's characters with a specified character, such as a star or hash. For example, you can hide all but the last four digits to preserve information for verification purposes.

steps.title: Tokenization based on encryption
steps.body: Replace the original value with an encrypted token using a key. If the same key and context are used, the same value will produce the same token, preserving relationships between records and enabling reversibility. Consider this when you need to restore the original value after receiving a model response.

steps.title: Bucketing and Date Movement
steps.body: Bucketing converts values into ranges. It's akin to using age groups instead of exact ages. Date shifting moves dates by a random number of days while preserving order and duration. It is suitable when you want to retain the usefulness of values for statistical or analytical purposes.

steps.title: Conclusion: Choose appropriately based on the objective.
steps.body: The transformation is determined based on whether the value can be reverted and how much of its utility remains. Values that the model does not need are either deleted or replaced; if restoration is required, tokenization is considered, and if used for analysis, bucketing or date shifting should be reviewed.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the conversion method, let me summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Review the core of the lesson and consider where filters are empty in my service.

paragraphs: Filters are applied to both the front and back of the model. The input filter reduces malicious inputs reaching the model, while the output filter screens the generated sentences before they are presented to the user. The result reads not just whether a flag is present, but also the category, confidence level, and error type.

Gateway-level filters consistently apply organizational policies independently of the model, while model-level security configurations are attached per model call and serve different purposes. Sensitive information is appropriately transformed—either by deletion, replacement, masking, tokenization, or bucketing—based on whether the information can be recovered and the value of the data.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Lowering the threshold may result in more requests being blocked, but it could also block legitimate requests. Set and adjust the value according to the service requirements. Logging the response code and message of blocked requests enables you to trace later which filter was triggered and provides justification for adjusting the threshold.

glossary.def: A service that classifies harmful content from text and images, returning flagged results and category-level confidence scores.
A Google Cloud service that checks prompts and responses to block malicious inputs, sensitive information, and policy violations.
This is a value that defines the probability from which blocking occurs by category.
A service that detects, classifies, and removes sensitive data, and de-identifies it through methods such as masking, tokenization, and deletion.

misconceptions.fact: The sentences generated by the model do not pass input validation. Outputs must also be validated before being presented to the user.

misconceptions.myth: The lower the threshold value, the better it always is.
misconceptions.fact: A low threshold can block low-probability requests, potentially preventing normal requests from reaching the service. Set it appropriately based on service requirements.

misconceptions.myth: If model-level settings are available, the gateway filter is unnecessary.
misconceptions.fact: The two devices have different scopes. The gateway filter applies organizational policies consistently regardless of the model, while model-level settings are attached per model call.

misconceptions.myth: If flagged is false, then it is safe.
misconceptions.fact: Confidence level, category, and error type must be read and separate criteria must be established according to the policy.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Filters are placed on both the front and back of the model.
The results read not only whether they are flagged, but also their confidence level and error type.
Gateway-level filtering and model-level safety settings have different roles.
Sensitive information selects the appropriate conversion type based on its purpose.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Which side, input or output, has a filter missing in our service?

checks.q: What is the difference between gateway-level filters (e.g., Model Armor) and model-level security settings?
options: The gateway filter checks input only, and model-level settings are checked only on output.
Since they have the same function, turning on one of them makes the other meaningless.
The gateway filter consistently applies organizational policies independent of the model, while model-level settings are attached per model call.
Model-level settings allow adjustments to all categories and can therefore be leveraged for child safety.
checks.explain: The gateway filter applies consistent policies to all agents passing through the gateway, independent of any model, while model-level safety settings are attached to model calls. The two serve different purposes.

wrong.0: Model Armor examines both the prompt and the response.
wrong.1: They have different roles due to their different application locations.
wrong.3: Regarding child safety, core features must always be disabled and adjustable.

checks.intro: Compare the differences between gateway filtering and model-level security settings. The results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. Since the application locations differ, they cannot replace each other.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Dividing input and output simply, or treating them as the same function, is an inappropriate choice.

checks.q:
Read the following code and select the place that should be fixed first.
resp = client.responses.create(model=MODEL, input=text, moderation={"model": "omni-moderation-latest"})
if resp.moderation.input.flagged: return refuse()
return resp.output_text
options: Remove the moderation option and handle input validation through a separate call only
Before displaying the generated output_text, verify the type and flagged status in resp.moderation.output.
When input.flagged is true, instead of calling refuse(), return the response unchanged.
Instead of output_text, return the input value to the user.
checks.explain: If moderation is applied, both input and output results are returned together; however, this code only examines the input. The model must display the generated sentence after verifying the output result, and it must also handle cases where the type is error.

wrong.0: Thanks to the options attached to the request, we are able to receive the output result. Removing them actually causes the output verification to disappear.
wrong.2: If input is flagged, the current operation is correct; the issue lies in the output side verification.
wrong.3: Returning input is not a response and does not solve the problem.

checks.intro: Start by selecting the place you should fix first in the moderation call code. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes, the sentence generated by the model must be shown after verifying the output result.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The input side operation is already correct. Please re-read the code to verify where the empty path is.
